shipped_originals.title_o: Impaired intuition in patients with major depressive disorder

blind_target.authors: Remmers, C., Topolinski, S., Buxton, A., Dietrich, D. E., & Michalak, J.
blind_target.title: The beneficial and detrimental effects of major depression on intuitive decision-making.
blind_target.evidence_quote:
The first hypothesis (H1) refers to the replica‐
bility of recently found intuition deficits in depression (Remmers et al., 2015; Remmers et
al., 2017). We hypothesized that patients with an acute episode of major depression are
less able to intuitively discriminate semantic coherence from semantic incoherence in the
JSCT than healthy controls.
blind_target.outcome_quote:
Overall the current study did not replicate findings from previous research regarding
intuitive  semantic  coherence  detection  deficits  in  depression.

blind_target.title: The architecture of intuition: Fluency and affect determine intuitive judgments of semantic and visual coherence and judgments of grammaticality in artificial grammar learning.
blind_target.evidence_quote:
Building up on basic research
(Topolinski & Strack, 2009a; Experiment 8) showing that healthy subjects are more
likely to judge triads to be coherent that consist of positive as compared to negative
words, we expected that this effect would also emerge for depressed patients.

Results did not reveal any effect of our fluency manipulation, and thus our hypothe‐

ses regarding fluency (H2) were not supported. As such, the current study could not
replicate previous results that bolstered the fluency model proposed by Topolinski and
Strack (2009a, 2009b).
blind_target.outcome_quote:
Results did not reveal any effect of our fluency manipulation, and thus our hypothe‐

ses regarding fluency (H2) were not supported. As such, the current study could not
replicate previous results that bolstered the fluency model proposed by Topolinski and
Strack (2009a, 2009b).

The results further showed that positive (vs. negative) valence triggered coherence

judgments (H3a) and that this effect was – in contrast to our hypothesis (H3b) – not
moderated by depression.

blind_target.title: The analysis of intuition: Processing fluency and affect in judgements of semantic coherence.
blind_target.evidence_quote:
Results did not reveal any effect of our fluency manipulation, and thus our hypothe‐

ses regarding fluency (H2) were not supported. As such, the current study could not
replicate previous results that bolstered the fluency model proposed by Topolinski and
Strack (2009a, 2009b).
blind_target.outcome_quote:
Results did not reveal any effect of our fluency manipulation, and thus our hypothe‐

ses regarding fluency (H2) were not supported. As such, the current study could not
replicate previous results that bolstered the fluency model proposed by Topolinski and
Strack (2009a, 2009b).

Our findings also revealed a significant interaction between valence and coherence

in the valence block (i.e., positive word triads that were coherent were most likely
to be judged as coherent in both groups). This finding indicates that positivity (con‐
veyed by positive valence in the current study) may lead to more accurate intuitive
judgments and is in line with previous research showing that not only “tonic” positive
affect (e.g., manipulated or freestanding positive mood; Balas et al., 2012; Bolte et al.,
2003) but also “phasic” positive affect (induced by the activation of positively valenced
memory content) can strengthen the accuracy of coherence judgments (Topolinski &
Strack, 2009b).

blind_target.authors: Santiago, J. L., Hanley, G. P., Moore, K., & Jin, C. S.
blind_target.title: The generality of interview-informed functional analyses: Systematic replications in school and home.
blind_target.evidence_quote: We replicated and extended Hanley et al. (2014) and Santiago et al. (2016).
blind_target.outcome_quote: We replicated and extended Hanley et al. (2014) and Santiago et al. (2016). We demonstrated the positive effects of stregthening FCRs, tolerance responses, and engagement with reinforcers identiﬁed via interview and analysis on problem behaviors with two young children diagnosed with ASD.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The authors explicitly state that they replicated and extended both named studies, and describe positive treatment effects. This overall verdict covers both targets.

shipped_originals.title_o: When cheating would make you a cheater: Implicating the self prevents unethical behavior.

blind_target.evidence_quote: Previous research has found that negative-valence appeals relating to the self (Don't be a cheater) are more effective at reducing unethical behaviour than appeals relating to behaviour (Don't cheat). We aimed to replicate these findings and examine whether positive-valence appeals relating to the self (Be an honest person) and to behaviour (Answer honestly) could have a similar effect.
blind_target.outcome_quote: A meta-analysis of the five experiments revealed a small effect of the self-appeals relative to the behaviour-appeals.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The abstract states the original self-appeal advantage and reports the same advantage in the aggregate of the five new experiments. Smaller effects do not change success. Citation identity cannot be established from the abstract.
